Subject: Concurrency saturation & driver mapping — test methodology ask

Hi Tessa,

Thanks for taking this RFP section. We need a concise, reproducible description of how Redwood measures concurrency saturation and maps client-side concurrency (threads/clients) to observed throughput and tail latency. Our procurement and engineering teams want:

- The exact warm-up sequence you run before sampling (durations, ramp rates).
- Request shape templates (token length distributions, prompt vs completion ratios).
- How you account for KV-cache warm state and prefix caching in results.
- The metrics exposed (GPU util, scheduler queue depth, p50/p95/p99 latency, backpressure events) and how long each is sampled.
- Any non-deterministic effects (GC pauses, tokenization variance) and mitigation.

We're planning two test modes: long-tail steady-state (45min) and bursty short spikes (30s spikes to peak) to validate both steady and transient behavior.

Can you respond with a test-methodology blurb and a small mapping table (client concurrency -> steady QPS -> p99) and any caveats? If you have a CSV we can ingest for our evaluation automation, that'd be ideal.

Best,
Sarah

Sarah — thanks for the clear list. I attached a concise CSV and a short runbook PDF that encode our canonical approach. High level summary below, then CSV notes.

High-level methodology (summary):
- Environment: dedicated Redwood Dedicated pool, NVIDIA H100x2 per pod, Q4 2026 kernel stack. Model variant: open-llm-family-13B (FP16 + 4-bit quantized candidate for comparison).
- Warm-up: 6 minute progressive warm-up: 2m @ 10% target QPS, 2m @ 40% target QPS, 2m @ 80% target QPS. For short spike tests we do a 90s pre-warm (10s ramp -> 80% hold).
- Workload templates: we provide three request profiles in CSV (short: 16 tokens prompt / 32 tokens completion; medium: 64/128; long: 256/256). Mix is 60% short, 30% medium, 10% long unless you ask otherwise.
- KV/prefix cache handling: we measure two curves — cold (no KV cache) and warmed (single-client run-through to populate KV for common prefixes). CSV has separate rows for COLD/WARM.
- Sampling windows: steady-state samples over 45 minutes after warm-up; report 1m sliding percentiles (p50/p90/p95/p99/p999), GPU util, memory headroom, scheduler queue depth distribution, and retry/backpressure counts.
- Concurrency sweep: we increment concurrent client threads in steps (1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256) with fixed per-client request rate to target a theoretical QPS per concurrency. For each step we hold for 3 minutes (plus a 30s buffer) to capture transient.
- Burst tests: 30s spike durations from baseline to target peak; measure time-to-restore and p99 amplification factor.

Caveats:
- Quantization (4-bit) can change per-token CPU/GPU kernel paths and usually improves steady throughput but can increase occasional p99 jitter due to kernel selection in our runtime; we report both variants.
- Autoscale and pre-warming policies change the first-second tail in hosted environments — Dedicated baseline removes autoscale variability, but if you run on shared clusters results will differ.
- Tokenization variance: we recommend running using our provided tokenization mapping tool to ensure the same detokenization distribution.

CSV notes (concurrency-matrix.csv):
- Columns: test_id, mode (COLD|WARM), concurrency, steady_qps, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, p999_ms, gpu_util_pct, avg_queue_depth, retries, notes
- Each test_id maps to a run command in runbook-warmup-and-ramp.pdf we attached.

I attached the CSV mapping with our canonical numbers from a recent run. Let us know if you want a different model variant or a probabilistic token mix.

Cheers,

Sarah — short answers with config snippets you can apply in your harness: 

1) KV warm strategy: we run two variants in our published CSV —
   - CLIENT_LINEAR: single client walks a hot prefix set (100 keys) sequentially until KV cache hit ratio > 90%. This produces the most optimistic warm curve.
   - SHALLOW_PARALLEL: 128 simulated clients each issue 5 short-prefix queries to mimic many users with recent small contexts; this usually yields the realistic conversational warm state and slightly higher p99 under warm runs. We included both rows in the CSV.

2) Time-to-restore: we report both metrics. The primary is time-to-95pct-qps (how long until throughput returns to 95% baseline). Secondary is time-to-latency-baseline (p95 back to within 10% of steady p95). Both are in the runbook for how we compute.

3) Batching: in the CSV canonical numbers batching was enabled with a conservative grouping policy (max_batch_tokens=2048, max_batch_size=8, max_latency_ms=8). We also include a BATCHING_DISABLED row set so you can compare. Batching reduces per-token GPU busy time but can artificially hurt single-request tail if batching latency windows are long; we highlight that in the notes column.

Run commands (examples, see runbook):
- ./run_benchmark --model open-llm-family-13B --variant fp16 --concurrency 64 --warm-mode SHALLOW_PARALLEL --duration 180 --batching enabled --out results/64_shallow_parallel.csv
- ./run_benchmark --model open-llm-family-13B --variant 4bit --concurrency 64 --warm-mode CLIENT_LINEAR --duration 180 --batching disabled --out results/64_linear_4bit.csv

If you want, Monica can schedule a joint run with your harness next week and we can watch metrics (nvidia-smi, pod-level traces, and our tracing agent) to debug the p99 jump.
